title: The Psalms of the Prophet's family
word: The Psalms of the Prophet's family
hookLine: Imam Ali Zayn al-Abidin's prayers, treasured by Shia Muslims and read by many others
tomorrow: what do you ask God for, when it comes to your parents?

cards: Some families keep a box of a grandmother's handwritten recipes, grease-spotted and annotated. Some keep her prayers. This book is that kind of inheritance.
Ali, the son of Husayn and great-grandson of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, survived Karbala, a battle where his father and much of his family were killed.
He's remembered as Zayn al-Abidin, the adornment of the worshippers. His prayers were gathered and kept. And tradition gives the book a striking nickname: the Psalms of the Prophet's family.

teach.b: The book is al-Sahifa al-Sajjadiyya, the pages of the one who prostrates. Shia Muslims treasure it, and many Sunni readers know and read it too.
It's a book of whole prayers, for mornings and evenings, for sickness and repentance, for parents, neighbors and children, for when rain comes and when a debt weighs on you.
Today's question is an old one: what do you say to God when your own words run out? The Sahifa's answer is, borrow some.

teach.h: A NEIGHBOR: OUT OF THE DEPTHS.
teach.b: Here's where a neighbor tradition says the same thing in its own words. Jews and Christians have prayed the Book of Psalms for every state of the heart.

Psalm 130 opens, in the King James Version: Out of the depths have I cried unto thee, O LORD. That's what shared looks like: a family of old prayers, kept so that people in the depths have words ready.
Muslims know the Psalms too; the Qur'an says God gave David the Zabur. And here's the honest difference.
For Jews and Christians, the Psalms are scripture. For Muslims, the Sahifa isn't.
Its prayers come from a holy man of the Prophet's family; the Qur'an alone is God's word. So the nickname names a likeness in use, not in rank.
Two traditions, each with a book that lends words to people who've lost theirs. Prayers of the family.

how: Shia Muslims recite prayers from al-Sahifa al-Sajjadiyya at home and in gatherings, some on particular days and occasions; Sunni readers also read and quote it.

games.why: a likeness in use, not in rank: both lend words to people who've lost theirs, and they hold different places in each tradition.

practice: Take a pen and copy one line of an old prayer you know by heart, from your own tradition or any you love, slowly, by hand. Notice which word your pen slows down on.
Then read the line once, quietly, as if someone in your family had written it for you.

wordCard.voice: The Psalms of the Prophet's family: tradition's name for al-Sahifa al-Sajjadiyya, the prayers of Zayn al-Abidin.

orig.note: Arabic: the pages of al-Sajjad, the one who prostrates; Zayn al-Abidin's book of prayers.

carryVoice: For the days your own words won't come: prayers of the family, kept for exactly that. The Sahifa's first page, turned.
